extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys/agents, culture collections (potential IDAs), and industrial property offices
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the requirements, procedures and safeguards for depositing microorganisms under the Budapest Treaty so that a single deposit can satisfy patent disclosure requirements across Contracting States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be described in sufficient detail to permit a person skilled in the art to repeat the effect of the invention; the disclosure should enable the average expert with appropriate facilities to reproduce the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure is normally achieved by a written description supplemented where necessary by drawings. If the invention involves a new microorganism not available to the public, written disclosure alone may be insufficient because repeatability often cannot be ensured by description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit as supplement to written disclosure for microorganisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Where repeatability cannot be ensured by written description alone (e.g., organisms isolated from soil or modified by mutation and selection), the microorganism itself may be considered an essential part of the disclosure and depositing the microorganism in a recognized culture collection should supplement the written disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many national patent offices either require or recommend such a deposit so that the culture collection can make the microorganism available to the public at the appropriate point in the patenting procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of single deposit by Contracting States (single-deposit principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposit made with any recognized International Depositary Authority (IDA) shall be recognized as valid for patent purposes by all Contracting States that allow or require deposit for patent procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids multiple deposits in several countries and makes one deposit serve the purposes of all deposits that would otherwise be needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility and nomination of International Depositary Authorities (IDAs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any culture collection can become an IDA if it has been formally nominated by the Contracting State in whose territory it is located and that Contracting State furnishes solemn assurances that the collection complies and will continue to comply with Treaty and Regulations requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An intergovernmental industrial property organization which files the relevant declaration may likewise furnish assurances for a collection on a member State’s territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core assurances required from an IDA
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important assurances are that the IDA will be available on the same terms to any depositor, that it will accept and store microorganisms deposited for the full period specified by the Treaty, and that it will furnish samples of deposited microorganisms only to those entitled to receive them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These assurances underpin recognition of deposits made in that IDA by Contracting States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of storage requirement for deposits
rubrics_metrics.description: IDAs must store deposited microorganisms for at least 30 years or five years after the most recent request for a sample, whichever is later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a minimum storage obligation laid down in the Regulations under the Treaty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures and conditions for furnishing samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations set out who may receive samples and the mechanisms for furnishing them: samples may be furnished at any time to the depositor, to anyone with the depositor's written authorization, and to any 'interested' industrial property office (i.e., one dealing with a patent application concerning the deposited microorganism and which provides the IDA with a declaration to that effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In other cases national law determines when, to whom and under what conditions samples are furnished. Because IDAs may not know national laws, the Regulations require third-party requests to be made on a form on which the relevant industrial property office certifies entitlement. Alternatively, industrial property offices may notify IDAs of accession numbers of microorganisms referred to in patents it has granted and published, making them available to anyone without certification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of deposit is governed by national law
rubrics_metrics.description: The Regulations do not address the timing of deposit; timing is left entirely to the relevant national law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, applicants must check applicable national patent law to determine when deposit must be made for that jurisdiction's patent procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards against loss and non-availability of deposits
rubrics_metrics.description: IDAs must have the expertise and facilities necessary to keep microorganisms viable and uncontaminated throughout the storage period. If an IDA becomes unable to furnish samples, a new deposit of the same organism can be made and can benefit from the date of deposit of the original. If an IDA ceases to function, deposited microorganisms shall be transferred to another IDA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These provisions guard against loss of availability that would undermine the disclosure function of the deposit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad interpretation of 'microorganism' for Treaty purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'microorganism' is not defined in the Treaty so it may be interpreted broadly; whether an entity is technically a microorganism matters less than whether deposit is necessary for disclosure and whether an IDA will accept it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical examples include acceptance of tissue cultures and plasmids under the Treaty, even if not microorganisms in the strict sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intergovernmental organizations may accept Treaty provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: An intergovernmental industrial property organization (e.g., the European Patent Office) may file a formal declaration with the WIPO Director General accepting the Treaty and Regulations for its own patent purposes, in which case it must recognize deposits made in any IDA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows non-State organizations with patent-granting competence to participate in the single-deposit recognition framework.
